body:
Warm welcome to Basil Chatha , our newest cohost from the Forward Deployed side of the AI Engineering world! We’ll be ramping up a new show with him and couldn’t pass up an interview with Modal’s CEO Eric on the occasion of their monster Series D!

Two years ago, we spoke with Erik Bernhardsson about his vision for truly serverless AI infrastructure: developers should be able to run code without provisioning clusters, predicting load, or paying for idle resources. CTO Akshat then joined us to talk about Modal’s infra primitives and stack to offer those primitives and agent experience.

A lot has changed in the past 5 months. Since their 5B series C, Modal now reports it crossed 1 billion in annualized run rate , raised a 750 million Series D at a 16B valuation , and has spun up nearly three billion sandboxes. In this conversation, Erik joins Vibhu to explain the infrastructure and economics behind that growth—and why demand for compute rarely looks like the contracts used to buy it.

Watch the full conversation on YouTube →

## GPU demand isn’t rectangular

A typical capacity contract gives a customer a fixed number of GPUs for a fixed period. Plot capacity against time and you get a rectangle. Real workloads behave differently: they grow, spike, and fall throughout the day. Buy enough for the peak and you pay for idle hardware; buy less and you risk missing demand.

Erik describes Modal’s bet as a kind of duration transformation: pool demand across thousands of customers, secure capacity underneath, and let each customer use what they need when they need it. The smoother the aggregate demand, the more useful that pool can be. It’s a useful companion to our conversation with SF Compute’s Evan Conrad : Evan focuses on making capacity tradeable; Erik focuses on making it usable in smaller, elastic slices.

There is a financial risk on the other side. If a provider locks in capacity at today’s prices and GPU prices later fall, it can be left holding expensive supply. Erik says he doesn’t expect an imminent collapse, but thinks the possibility matters when building the business. Jump to the GPU price discussion →

## The sandbox that almost didn’t make it

Modal launched sandboxes after Erik and cofounder Akshat Bubna noticed that language models could generate code—and that someone would need a place to run it. Early adoption was modest enough that the team discussed shutting the product down. Then coding agents, background agents, and reinforcement learning created new demand. Erik says sandboxes have grown to roughly a third of Modal’s revenue, a result he didn’t predict at launch.

That growth also changes what infrastructure has to do. An agent may create an environment, run code, inspect the result, and try again many times. The latency of starting and restoring those environments becomes part of the experience. In our recent interview with Akshat , we explored this shift from developer experience to agent experience; here Erik adds the product and business story. Jump to the sandbox discussion →

## Fast startup is an infrastructure feature

Elasticity only works if capacity can arrive quickly enough to matter. Modal’s serverless GPU write-up describes the machinery: a buffer of available GPUs, a custom filesystem, process checkpointing, and GPU memory snapshots. Those pieces reduce the work needed to bring another model replica online. It is a concrete example of how infrastructure decisions show up in an application’s responsiveness and cost.

We also discuss Erik’s path from Spotify’s recommendation system to Modal, how the company buys compute, alternatives to NVIDIA, forward-deployed engineers, and why code review is optional at Modal. Jump to engineering culture →

And most of that time was building basically from scratch and music recommendation system and built up a small team and we launched a bunch of features like related artists and Discover Weekly and a bunch of other stuff. Mortgages. Okay. Yeah. How did you get into that?

Like this guy, Zach Frankel, who I didn’t know at that time, ended up recruiting me to Better as a CTO and the company was 10 people. And, you know, for whatever reason, you know, the founder of Vishal, very interesting guy, very, very smart, a little crazy in mostly positive ways. We got very well along. So we, yeah, we started building it in 2015 and I spent five years growing that company and then, you know, eventually turned out that doing mortgages is pretty hard and, you know, interest rates went up very quickly after the pandemic and that cost a lot of issues at the company. But by then I had already left. That was like 2020, 2021 when you left? Yeah, something like that. Yeah. So, OK, you left before you had the idea for a model or you left and then you started? I was kind of just, you know, during the pandemic, I sort of almost took like a sabbatical at two kids. But actually both, you know, model was like, I think the 30 I built that I got, you know, that so there were like a few attempts before then that went nowhere.

You kind of need to start over a little bit from scratch. So I guess like the auto scaling, like did you, did you see any like weird behaviors on the platform? Like was there anything that like broke while you guys were scaling? I mean, capacity is always from time to time been, been a challenge. Like we always thought of like our capacity management as like one big pull. Like it’s like one big pull over the entire world. Like we don’t think of it as like separate clusters running in each region. And so that was like one of the like very consequential decisions we made early to kind of think about it that way. So I don’t know if there’s like been like, you know, specific issues. I mean, we’ve obviously had bugs and, you know, outages and I hate, you know, as much as I, you know, would love for a model to be a hundred percent uptime, you know, and I think recently we’ve basically hit four or five nines, but throughout the history of model, of course, we’ve had, you know, some run up against scaling issues. 13:30 Like do you also buy any infrastructure? No, let’s talk a bit about like cloud capacity. Because I think it’s actually changed a lot. So that, that, that model worked really well until we started running up again. And in many cases, in order to get the capacity we want, like we, we have to go into, you know, three plus year deals and you have to pay a meaningful amount of money upfront. And you’re locking in pricing on a three year term, right?

15:00 So, you know, like, and, and, and so we have to spend the entire, you know, last six to nine months, like, you know, kind of rethinking how we get capacity. We’ve had to build a whole engineering team, basically 10 people just like managing like bare metal capacity from all over the world and dealing with network issues and bad drives and GPUs falling off the bus and, and all these things. We don’t own capacity. We rent all the capacity so far, um, you know, on, on, on typically this three year deals. And that’s like a big decision. Like, should we buy, should, should we, you know, or should we keep renting? I’m actually like not like mega dogmatic about it. I think renting is nice because there’s a certain amount of capital efficiency to it. If you’re buying, you know, like, I mean, first of all, there’s not this like operational complexity of it. Like you have to, you know, deal with vendors and suppliers and, and, you know, power and, and, and cables and all kinds of stuff. But there’s also, you know, financial complexity to it. Like, how do you fund it? Like, should you raise equity, you know, and, and you can raise a billion dollars and go buy hardware for it. That’s a very dilutive way to do it. Um, you can raise debt, but you know, if you raise that, you know, you typically want to have like locked in long-term revenue to, to, to pay the interest rates. That’s also not trivial. But you know, like we look at the economics, we look at, uh, the operational

16:30 complexity, we look at the risks. Uh, it’s a complex trade-off and, and we’re open to, to, to buying. We’ll, we’ll sort of, there’s other constructs too. Like we’re, it’s to get the capacity we need for, for 2027. It’s going to take a lot of work on, on, you know, going a lot of different avenues to, to lock it up. So do you have to hire a lot of like finance people to do all this stuff or not? Really? You know, I’ve had to spend a lot of time on this and we’ve had to, to, to spend a lot of time on this. I wouldn’t want to like, I would rather focus on being, you know, like a very lean software company, like doing the things we’re good at. I don’t think it’s good in general for software companies to own hard assets. You know, in the same way as like, should you own your office? Like I don’t think that’s necessarily the right solution for most companies. But of course, like in order to get the capacity you want, like, you know, everything is on the table. Yeah. And I guess the supply is going to be constrained for a while.

And I do think it’s worth kind of reflecting on that. It’s like the normal state of hardware is like, it’s like out of like gravity. Like eventually, hardware prices always go down. So we’re a little bit in like a weird sort of period of time where like hardware prices are going up. And, you know, it’s hard to say, you know, how long this is going to last, you know, could be another six months, could be another 36 months. Like it’s really hard to know how long. But I fundamentally don’t know if like it’s true to say, like, you know, you need to buy capacity in order to me, that’s a little bit to sort of almost like the great toilet paper shortage of the pandemic or whatever. Right. Like, you know, at least this like, you know, run on the bank type situations. And, but that being said, like, you know, capacity is going to be tight for a while. And, you know, prices are going up. And, you know, luckily, I think, you know, it’s not even necessarily bad for us. If prices go up, because, because, you know, scarcity also means like we can

19:30 charge more from our customers. And, you know, and the fact that we have a lot of reservations locked in at a rate means like, to some extent, we’re effectively like long GPU prices already. So I don’t necessarily worry too much about prices going up. I do worry more about actually prices collapsing. I don’t think that’s going to happen anytime soon. But I think that would be a quite bad thing for a lot of the players in the market. Why would that be bad? I think it would be bad for if, for anyone who’s locked in a lot of supply. Yeah. Because they paid way too much and they paid too much, you know, so there’s a risk of buying at the top, right? And again, like, I don’t worry about that much. Like, I don’t think it’s going to be like, you know, it’s going to happen anytime soon. But like, you know, like I said, like hardware prices in the very long run, they tend to go down. And so it’s, it’s worth, you know, reflecting on that, right? Right. Like right now, I think, I think your, your capacity is constrained and, and that leads to sort of, you know, in economic terms, there’s a scarcity rent, right? Like who captured the scarcity rent? I think the primarily goes to two places, mostly Nvidia, but of course, but also to some extent, Neoclouds, like Neoclouds and in general, like, you know, anyone owning capacity has better economics. Like that’s undeniably true today with capacity being constrained. Long term, you know, in the very long run, I don’t think that’s necessarily entirely true, right? Like there’s always going to be a little bit of a premium you can get from owning GPUs, but is it worth the risk? You know, is it worth the risk of like holding this like very expensive
